title: Operating Contract for the System You Assembled
objective: Assemble a path that includes at least partitioning or replication plus an outbox-or-broker hop, run a three-class failure playbook you wrote before the run, and publish a falsifiable operating contract covering what is refused, what is retried, what can be lost, and which trace or query proves each case.
whyThisMatters: Every earlier task isolated one mechanism. A mid-to-senior engineer is trusted when those mechanisms sit in one path and the contract still holds. The SWE curriculum ends distributed systems with sagas and a Raft lab. This task ends with a contract a mentor could page you on.
evidence: A playbook file committed before the runs, naming three failure classes, the expected client result, the expected durable result, and the telemetry query that would confirm each
Captured runs for all three classes, each with client output, a state query (SQL, store GET, or Kafka consume), and a trace or metric excerpt matching the playbook query
The operating-contract README: numbered, falsifiable rules only — no 'highly available' or 'best effort'
Git history of the assembled path (not a new greenfield demo) showing playbook, then runs, then contract edits after mismatches
Reflection notes answering the task questions
acceptanceCriteria: The assembled path includes (a) more than one process that owns data (replicas or shards) and (b) an asynchronous hop (outbox, Kafka, or RabbitMQ); a single process with an in-memory queue does not count.
The playbook commit precedes the first run commit or the playbook file carries timestamps earlier than the run logs for all three classes.
Each of the three captured runs includes the playbook's confirmation query (trace, SQL, or consume) and a pass/fail against the predicted client result and predicted durable result.

The operating contract is a list of falsifiable rules that mention at least: refuse vs timeout bounds, a named loss case (or an explicit 'no acked write is lost' with the setting that makes it true), and the telemetry signal used to classify accepted-then-lost.
